levelMapping: L4 = 'Software Engineer' (recruiters call it SWE II / IC4) ≈ Google L4 / Amazon SDE II; typical band is ~2–5 YOE (Levels.fyi shows L4 at ~2–3 YOE; one L4 offer went to a 3-YOE Microsoft engineer, another L4 loop to a Google L4 with 1.6 YOE). L5 = Senior (≈ Google L5). Databricks is known for NOT up-levelling via interview and for down-levelling (L6→L5, L5→L4 reported); a 3.3-YOE candidate should expect to be slotted at L4 and confirm with the recruiter whether the loop includes an Architecture (HLD) round — several 2025 reports say L4 loops have NO Architecture round, only coding/algorithms/system-programming + HM. India (Bengaluru) hires L3 (campus), L4 and L5; the Bengaluru office opened ~2023–24 and is described as small and picky.

process.summary: Recruiter screen → 1-hour technical phone screen (CoderPad, one deep practical problem with multi-part follow-ups; candidates are sometimes offered a choice between an Algorithms screen and an Architecture screen) → team matching (HM calls) → virtual onsite of 4–6 one-hour rounds drawn from Databricks' named modules: Coding (production-quality, run the tests), Algorithms (optimal solution), System Programming (single-node LLD + concurrency in pseudocode/real code), Architecture (HLD, CoderPad Draw; often omitted at L4), Domain Deep Dive (senior+), Cross-Functional/Hiring Manager (behavioral) → Hiring Committee → 3 references (actually called, plus well-documented 'backdoor' references) → offer. The loop is harder than most: the question bank is small but every question is multi-part and 'practical' (custom data structures, KV stores, QPS/hit counters, CIDR firewalls, file-system trees, snapshot iterators, Fibonacci trees, grid routing with transport modes), and interviewers expect compiling, tested, clean code. Karat is NOT used for experienced SWE hiring in 2025–26 (it appeared only in old 2019–2020 new-grad/intern reports); the phone screen is run by a Databricks engineer.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.what: Background, motivation, role/team fit; recruiter asks why you left each company and whether you were promoted (2026 report). Profile then goes to engineering leads / HMs who may 'park' it. Recruiter sends a PDF describing each round — read it.
rounds.probes: Role understanding (don't pitch AI/ML interest for an infra role), tenure/promotion history (short stints have cancelled onsites), level expectations (no up-levelling).

rounds.name: Technical phone screen
rounds.what: One long, multi-part problem in CoderPad with a Databricks engineer (often from Amsterdam/US for India candidates). Expect a long problem statement (5 min just to read), a design-flavoured data structure (KV store with QPS/load metrics, snapshot-set iterator, CIDR firewall, Fibonacci-tree path, grid commute with transport modes, revenue/referral tracker, file-encryption tree) and 1–3 follow-ups that change constraints. Since 2026 some candidates are offered an Architecture-style screen instead (bookstore price aggregator, music playlist service).
rounds.probes: Explain the plan and invariants before coding; code must compile and pass self-written tests; clarify time source / QPS semantics; complexity of each follow-up; language fluency (knowing how to get system time in ms, string parsing). A second screen is sometimes granted if the team is undecided.

rounds.name: Hiring manager / team-matching call
rounds.what: Often happens before the onsite in India (HM is an elimination round there) and again after; discussion of past projects, challenges, why Databricks. Multiple HM chats possible while team-matching.
rounds.probes: Technical depth on your own project, measurable impact ('which queries, before/after numbers'), cross-functional work, production incidents end to end, when you escalated.

rounds.name: Onsite: Coding
rounds.what: Implementation-focused, production-quality code with tests and edge cases; typically a class/API to build out in stages (generalized Tic-Tac-Toe m×n with k-in-a-row + random/AI move, RLE + bit-packing codec, lazily-evaluated array, referral-credit tracker, cover/delete-index string problem, circuit breaker for leader/follower DB, CachedFile range cache).
rounds.probes: Run the code mid-way, handle invalid input, clean structure (helper functions, naming), Big-O, extend when requirements shift; interviewers may interrupt and ask for explanation under time pressure.

rounds.name: Onsite: Algorithms
rounds.what: Optimal-solution round. Databricks-flavoured graph/grid/tree problems: grid shortest path with transport modes (BFS per mode, then Dijkstra with mode in state), Fibonacci-tree path, topological sort / build-pipeline bottlenecks, web crawler with depth limit, House Robber I→II, anagram window (LC 438), hit counter / QPS. Sometimes two interviewers.
rounds.probes: Why not Dijkstra when BFS suffices (and vice versa), O(n) constraints on follow-ups (e.g., duplicate handling without sorting), complexity analysis, tests you'd write.

rounds.name: Onsite: System Programming (LLD + concurrency)
rounds.what: Databricks' signature round. Single-machine component design in pseudocode or real code: thread-safe durable event/log writer with batching + fsync, concurrent KV store with batch writes, thread-safe LRU/TTL cache with sharded locks, bounded producer–consumer queue / thread pool, multithreaded web crawler, durable single-node KV store (WAL, recovery), range-aware file cache. Both single-threaded and multi-threaded versions are expected.
rounds.probes: Which locks, how small is the critical section, condition variables vs. busy-wait, deadlock avoidance (lock ordering), why HashMap isn't thread-safe / how ConcurrentHashMap works, CAS, fsync semantics and durability-before-ack, batching to amortize syscalls, promise/future to unblock writers, ordering guarantees, failure recovery, Python GIL caveats if you use Python.

rounds.name: Onsite: Architecture (HLD)
rounds.what: Classic end-to-end system design on CoderPad Draw. Frequent prompts: online bookstore / lowest-price book aggregator fanning out to hundreds of sellers, chat/Slack-like messaging (with deletion semantics), payment processing (Visa-like; game-platform credit card with refunds), distributed job scheduler, music playlist service, hierarchical/distributed file system, rate limiter at scale. Reported as OFTEN ABSENT at L4 (replaced by a second coding round) and present at L5+.
rounds.probes: Failure modes over happy path (DB insert succeeds but queue publish fails → transactional outbox; at-least-once duplicates → idempotent consumers), batching external fetches, POST vs GET, partial results on timeouts, caching/freshness, concurrency of transactions, back-of-envelope numbers.

rounds.name: Onsite: Cross-functional / behavioral
rounds.what: With an engineering leader (sometimes a director or senior architect). Several small questions across 4–5 'topics' (e.g., navigating conflict, disputed feedback, proudest project, technical disagreement, motivation) rather than one long story; a second behavioral may occur with the HM.
rounds.probes: Consistency and depth on one project (challenges → disagreements → mentoring → leading without authority), no company jargon, cross-team collaboration, handling critical feedback; some interviewers cut off technical detail — keep answers focused.

rounds.name: Hiring committee + references
rounds.what: Interviewer scores (e.g., LH/H) go to an HC; 'strong hire' feedback can still be reversed. Recruiter then asks for 3 references (ex-manager, TL/peers) who are actually called (15–45 min each). Multiple 2025–26 reports of 'backdoor' references via LinkedIn connections and even requests for performance-review evidence; rejections at this stage are common.
rounds.probes: Pick references who will speak concretely; avoid listing your current manager; be aware your current employer may hear you're interviewing.

process.indiaNotes: Bengaluru (opened ~2023) runs the same module-based loop, usually fully virtual, with interviewers mixed from India, Amsterdam and the US (late-night slots for India candidates). India L4/SDE-2 loops reported in 2023–2026: phone screen (KV store with 5-min get/put load; top-K stream variant; CIDR firewall; revenue/referral service) → 2 coding/algorithms rounds (hit counter with system time → circular array; circuit breaker for leader/follower DB as LLD; web crawler with depth K + multithreading; cover/delete-index; CIDR first-match + trie + whole-block query) → one 'design' round that is single-machine durable KV store with pseudocode (not distributed) → behavioral/HM → team matching → HC with 3 references. HM is often an elimination round BEFORE the technical rounds in India. Full process can take 1–4 months; one Bengaluru candidate was rejected with 'reapply in 8 months'. Campus (IIIT/IIT) SWE hiring is 2–3 pure DSA rounds + HM (tree traversal of target nodes, server-cost DP, DP/tree problems). India L4 comp data points: ~95L–1Cr TC quoted for a 3-YOE L4 in 2025; new-grad 36L base + RSUs; offers are not revised after initial numbers. Cooldown after a phone-screen fail is ~1 year, no retry.
process.timeline: Phone-screen result in 1–4 days; onsite scheduled 1–3 weeks later (4–6 rounds over 1–2 days); onsite feedback in ~3–7 days; then references + HC + team match add 2–3 weeks. Typical 4–8 weeks end to end, India loops have taken up to 4 months; Databricks itself quotes feedback within 48h of the final round.
tips: Treat the phone screen like an onsite: one hard, multi-part practical problem with a long statement — read it fully, restate it, and ask about the time source / QPS definition / ordering before coding.

Every question has multiple parts; a Databricks interviewer on Blind said candidates fail by spending the whole hour on the warm-up. Get part 1 working fast with helper functions so follow-ups change one function.

Write and run your own tests in CoderPad; several rejections cite 'forgot to write tests', 'code not clean enough' or a missed edge case (e.g., QPS divisor during the first seconds of uptime = min(uptime, 300)).

Drill the Databricks question bank patterns (they repeat with twists): KV store + QPS/hit counter (deque vs ring buffer/time buckets), snapshot-set iterator (versioned/persistent set), CIDR/IP firewall (first-match, trie, whole-block queries), Fibonacci-tree path (subtree sizes + preorder numbering → LCA), grid commute with transport modes (BFS per mode → Dijkstra with mode in state + switch penalty), file-encryption tree DP, RLE/bit-packing codec, generalized Tic-Tac-Toe, lazy array, revenue/referral least-k, cover/delete-index.

Prepare the System Programming round separately: thread-safe logger/event writer with batching + fsync + promise/future, bounded blocking queue, thread pool, sharded-lock LRU with TTL, multithreaded crawler; know locks, condition variables, semaphores, deadlock ordering, why HashMap is not thread-safe, CAS. 'The Little Book of Semaphores' is the community's go-to.

Databricks prefers correct, simple synchronization over clever lock-free code; if you use Python, state GIL limitations explicitly (recruiters confirm Python is fine since code need not compile in that round).

For Architecture/design screens, drill the bookstore/price-aggregator, chat/Slack, payment and job-scheduler prompts and especially failure modes (outbox pattern, idempotency, batching); batch writes/WAL batching came up in every design round of one Staff loop.
Pick one language you are fluent in (C++ candidates lost time on std::chrono/string functions; one was marked down for 'not fully familiar with C++'). Don't switch languages mid-interview.

Ask the recruiter which modules your loop has (L4 loops often lack Architecture) and whether a 'design' round expects code — Indian candidates were surprised when an 'HLD' round demanded code for each problem.
Line up 3 strong references before the onsite and avoid listing your current manager; expect reference calls of 15–45 min and possible backchannel checks.

Interviewer hints are strong signals: when told 'Dijkstra isn't needed' or 'integers are enough, no node struct', pivot immediately; but if a hint conflicts with a working approach, say so and compare complexity rather than silently switching.
process.notes: Platform: CoderPad (runnable code; Draw mode for architecture) over Google Meet. Language-agnostic but fluency is tested; Lombok and similar helpers unavailable. Some teams (full-stack, newer India teams) have used take-home assignments (e.g., weather-forecast API, CLI query parser, 3–5 h) and a CodeSignal OA appears for new-grad/intern pipelines (e.g., 4 problems in 70 min); experienced SWE loops in 2025–26 have no OA. Karat: historically used for new-grad/intern screens around 2019–2020 (three LC-easy questions, CS-fundamentals quiz); not reported for experienced hires since, so a 2026 L4 candidate should expect a Databricks engineer on the screen — still, be ready for quick fundamentals probes inside rounds (HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap locking, CAS, fsync/page cache, Python GIL). No system-design round for L4 in several 2025 US reports; L5 adds Architecture; L6+ adds Domain Deep Dive. Rejection cooldown ~12 months; no phone-screen retry, though some candidates were asked to redo one onsite round after a borderline concurrency round. Hiring Committee can reject despite strong-hire feedback; references are heavily weighted. Recruiting communication is frequently criticized (ghosting, cancelled onsites, reallocated headcount). The LLD list below is the System Programming/practical-coding round — Databricks runs it for every backend level including L4.

dsa.title: Key-value store with get/put load (QPS over last 5 minutes)
dsa.statement: Implement put(key, value), get(key) and measureGetLoad()/measurePutLoad() (or get_load()) returning the number or average rate of calls in the trailing 5-minute window using real system time. Variants: Design Hit Counter with system-time timestamps; QPS over arbitrary [start,end] ranges; report over 1h/1d/1w windows; many calls within one second.
dsa.variant: Interviewer expects circular array / per-second buckets (deque accepted but marked down); edge case: divisor must be min(uptime, 300) not 300; follow-ups: 300-day windows (hierarchical buckets), bursty vs sparse traffic (queue vs ring buffer), multiple calls per second (millisecond buckets), exact QPS over arbitrary ranges via binary search, approximate QPS with fixed-width buckets; testing requires injecting a fake clock.
dsa.evidence: The single most-reported Databricks screen/onsite question: Bangalore L4 phone screen (2024-05), India SDE-2 onsite (2023-11), SDE phone screen (2025-03), 1point3acres threads (2025), PracHub screens (2026-06 rejected on edge case; 2026-06/07 offer loop), Aarhus senior screen (2026-06), cleared-onsite report (2026-07).

dsa.title: IP/CIDR firewall — first-match ALLOW/DENY rules
dsa.statement: Given an ordered list of rules like (ALLOW, '192.168.100.0/24'), (DENY, '10.5.12.10/28'), (ALLOW, '1.2.3.4'), implement access_ok(ip) that returns the verdict of the FIRST matching rule (default DENY) and optionally the matching rule index. A bare IP is a /32; handle /0 and /32 masks. Loosely related to LC 751 (IP to CIDR) but the asked problem is rule matching.
dsa.variant: Follow-ups: query many IPs efficiently (binary trie / longest-prefix match), decide whether an entire CIDR block is fully allowed/denied/mixed (interval arithmetic), convert an IP range to minimal CIDRs, segment-tree over rules (new-grad 2026).
dsa.evidence: Phone screens for L4 and L5 (2024-09, 2025-02, 2025-06 offer loop, 2025-11 SSE screen), OA 2023, onsite DSA round in SDE-II loop (2026-02), Bangalore L4 technical round 1 (2024-05), new-grad onsite (2026-01). Candidates say it is asked 'regardless of level'.

dsa.title: Shortest path in a Fibonacci tree (preorder-numbered, implicit)
dsa.statement: Fibonacci trees are defined recursively: T0 is empty, T1 is a single node, Tn has a root whose left child is T(n-2) and right child is T(n-1). Nodes are numbered 0..size-1 by DFS preorder. Given order n and two node labels start and end, return the shortest path as a string of moves 'U' (up), 'L' (left), 'R' (right); e.g. fibPath(3,1,3) = 'URR', fibPath(5,3,7) = 'UURLR'. No node structure is given and you may not build the tree — use subtree sizes (size(Tn) = size(Tn-1)+size(Tn-2)+1) to compute the root-to-node paths and then combine via the lowest common ancestor.
dsa.variant: Follow-up: how does the solution change if nodes are numbered by in-order traversal? Interviewer hints: 'use the tree's properties', 'integers are enough', 'subtract subtree sizes from the target instead of passing a current-node parameter'. Expected O(order) time/space.
dsa.evidence: Screens: SDE-II India (2026-02), senior onsite loop tech screen (2026-04), PracHub screens (2025-11 rejected, 2026-05 ran out of time), Amsterdam screen (2026-08), new-grad finals (2025-12), SDE algorithm round (2025-03). Matches Stack Overflow question 76142856.

dsa.title: Optimal commute on a city grid with transport modes
dsa.statement: A 2D grid has 'S' (start), 'D' (destination), 'X' (blocked) and digits 1–4 for transport modes (walk/bike/car/train). Arrays time[] and cost[] give per-move time and cost for each mode. You move 4-directionally and, in the base version, must stay in one mode (only traverse cells of that mode). Return the mode giving the fastest S→D route; break ties by lowest cost; handle unreachable cases.
dsa.variant: Follow-up 1: allow switching modes with a fixed time penalty per switch (Dijkstra with state (time, cost, r, c, mode)). Follow-up 2: cap the number of switches. Follow-up (2025-10 screen): handle duplicates when comparing results across modes in O(n) without sorting. Interviewers often hint that BFS per mode suffices and Dijkstra is overkill for the base problem. A city-graph (non-grid) version with weighted edges also appears.
dsa.evidence: Phone screens 2025-02, 2025-10 (senior, rejected), 2026-04 (second screen), and onsite DSA II in the L4 offer loop (2025-06); 1point3acres 'Optimal Commute' threads; Glassdoor 'BFS chess/grid problem with follow-ups' (2026-08).

dsa.title: Snapshot set iterator (iterate a frozen view while mutating)
dsa.statement: Design a set with add(x), remove(x), contains(x) and iterator()/snapshot(): an iterator must yield exactly the elements present when it was created, even if the set is modified afterwards (adds/removes are visible to contains() immediately and to later iterators). Copying the whole set per snapshot is too slow; use versioned/persistent structures, per-element version logs, or an insertion-ordered list with tombstones. Related in spirit to LC 1146 Snapshot Array.
dsa.variant: Follow-ups: O(1) snapshot creation, memory with many live snapshots, deterministic insertion order for snapshots, 'make snapshot fetching faster' (bisect on version), interviewer may push per-key logs vs one shared log; must implement __iter__/hasNext/next correctly.
dsa.evidence: Phone screens 2025-06 (L4), 2026-04 (two PracHub reports), 2026-05 (ran out of time on bisect); onsite Coding 2 in senior loop (2026-04); older phone report 2022-03 'Custom Hashset'; Linkjob onsite report.

dsa.title: File-system tree: count encrypted files, then minimum encryption cost
dsa.statement: Given a Directory tree (directories contain sub-directories and Files with an isEncrypted flag), first return counts of encrypted and unencrypted files under a directory (DFS). Follow-up: two external APIs exist — encryptFile(path) costs requestTime + fileEncryptTime, encryptDirectory(path) costs requestTime + N*fileEncryptTime where N counts ALL files under it (already-encrypted ones too). Compute the minimum total time to encrypt every unencrypted file by choosing, per subtree, between one directory call and recursing into children.
dsa.variant: Recursive DP: cost(dir) = min(requestTime + totalFiles(dir)*fileTime, sum over children cost(child) + requestTime+fileTime per unencrypted direct file); discuss when batch beats individual calls.
dsa.evidence: L4 technical phone screen (2025-11), onsite Coding 1 in offer loop (2026-07), Linkjob onsite report (2026).

dsa.title: Generalized Tic-Tac-Toe (m×n board, k in a row) with AI/random move
dsa.statement: Implement TicTacToe(rows, cols, k) with move(row, col, player) returning -1 (invalid: out of bounds/occupied/game over), 0 (no winner) or the winning player when k consecutive marks align in any of 4 directions; only the newest move can create a win, so check O(k) around it. Variants: alternate turns automatically, print/snapshot the board after each move, report winner after every move, detect draw.
dsa.variant: Follow-ups: is_robot/getNextMove(player) returning a uniformly random empty cell efficiently on a huge board (track empty cells; Fenwick tree for k-th empty cell), a deterministic automatic opponent, forced-win detection via BFS/minimax on small boards.
dsa.evidence: Onsite DSA round in SDE-II loop (2026-02), onsite Coding 3 in offer loop (2026-07), L6→L5 onsite coding (2026-09), game-logic onsite (2026-09), L4 full-stack DSA round in India (2024-11, 'matrix game winning conditions'), interviewing.io 'variable-size tic-tac-toe'.

dsa.title: Streaming RLE + bit-packing encoder/decoder
dsa.statement: Build a codec for a stream of 32-bit signed integers that emits run-length blocks {value, count} for runs of at least RLE_MIN_RUN equal values and bit-packed blocks {bitWidth, count, words} for everything else, where bitWidth is the minimum two's-complement width across the chunk and values are packed LSB-first across 32-bit words (chunks capped at e.g. 128 values). Implement Encoder.add(int)/flush() and a Decoder that is an Iterator<Integer>; then decode back exactly. LC 900 (RLE Iterator) is the closest warm-up; the real question adds bit-packing and sign extension.
dsa.variant: Follow-ups: coverage audit of a test suite (INT_MIN/INT_MAX, negatives, empty input, alternating block types), minimizing RLE length with deletions, extending to 64-bit values, straddling word boundaries.
dsa.evidence: Onsite Coding 1 in senior loop (2026-04, 'strong hire'), Staff AI-platform loop coding round (2026-05), PracHub onsite entry (2025-12); OfferRetriever lists 'Encode And Decode' as Databricks.

dsa.title: Customer revenue service with referrals and least-k / top-k queries
dsa.statement: Implement insert(revenue) → new auto-increment customerId; insert(revenue, referrerId) → same, but also credit the revenue to the referrer; get_k_lowest_revenue(k, minRevenue) (or top-k above/below a threshold) → the k customers with least revenue among those having at least minRevenue. Maintain an ordered structure keyed by (revenue, id) for O(k log n) queries.
dsa.variant: Follow-ups: make the threshold query O(1)/O(k) (precompute at insert, O(n²) inserts); get_nested_referral(customerId, depth) summing revenue through indirect referrals up to depth — optimise space, then time; read-heavy vs write-heavy workloads; nested order/line-item revenue input.
dsa.evidence: Bangalore L4 second phone screen (2024-05, India interviewer), 2022 tech screen 'return K elements above a threshold', onsite referral-credits round (2026-09), Linkjob question bank; PracHub technical-screen follow-up (2026-02).

dsa.title: Cover a reference string with source blocks; delete an index and keep the cover maximal
dsa.statement: A string is represented as a 'cover': an ordered list of (start, end) index ranges into a source/reference string, e.g. source 'abc1234abcd', ref 'abcd123' → cover [(7,11),(3,6)]. Implement delete(cover, index) that removes the character at logical position index and returns a new valid cover (split the containing interval). Follow-up: the cover must stay 'maximal' — no two adjacent blocks may be mergeable into a block that still exists contiguously in the source; after a deletion you must check up to 3 neighbouring intervals (4 for insertion) and prove why.
dsa.variant: Also framed as warehouse shelves covering slot ranges where a picker removes the idx-th covered slot ('Remove Covered Point').
dsa.evidence: Bangalore L4 technical round 2 (2024-05, India interviewer) and onsite DSA I in the L4 offer loop (2025-06); OfferRetriever 'Remove Covered Point'.

dsa.title: Earliest anagram window / anagram check
dsa.statement: Given a long text and a shorter pattern, return the smallest start index where some permutation of the pattern occurs as a contiguous substring (−1 if none); fixed-size sliding window with character counts. Simpler variant asked at senior full-stack screen: are two strings anagrams.
dsa.variant: Probes on character set / UTF-8 handling, error returns for empty inputs, writing your own tests; return all start indices (LC 438) or just the first; LC 567 Permutation in String is the same idea.
dsa.evidence: Technical screens 2026-06 (PracHub) and mid-2026 senior full-stack screen; both LC 438 and LC 567 are in Databricks' tagged list.

dsa.title: Randomly connect N disjoint graphs into one connected graph (uniform over outcomes)
dsa.statement: You are given k node groups (each already connected), e.g. [[1],[2,3],[4,5,6]]. Repeatedly pick two different groups, pick one random node from each, and add an edge, until everything is connected using exactly k−1 edges. Every valid resulting connected graph (every spanning-tree shape over groups and every node choice) must be equally likely. Decide how to represent graphs and return the list of added edges.
dsa.variant: Candidates note that union-find/Kruskal with random order does NOT yield a uniform random spanning tree; interviewer works through hints. Earlier version: merge n connected graphs into one chain, each ordering equally likely.
dsa.evidence: Phone screens 2025-01 (San Francisco) and 2026-04 (first of two screens, 'really hard'); Linkjob follow-up phone round.

dsa.title: Lazily evaluated array (SluggishArray): chained map + indexOf
dsa.statement: Implement a LazyArray/SluggishArray class wrapping an int array with map(f) that records a transformation and returns a new lazy array (chainable: arr.map(f).map(g)), and indexOf(value) that returns the first index whose element equals value after all pending functions are applied. Functions must be applied lazily; stop early at the first match rather than materialising the whole array.
dsa.variant: Follow-ups: only evaluate as far as needed (short-circuit), prove laziness with a mock/counting wrapper, enumerate test cases; interviewer noted a candidate 'did not finish the initial implementation' (Bengaluru L4 2024-10).
dsa.evidence: Bengaluru L4 coding round (2024-10, Glassdoor), India L5 round 1 (2023-11), Linkjob bank, OfferRetriever 'Design Lazy Array', PracHub 'lazy array and KV store' (2026-01).

dsa.title: Build-pipeline bottlenecks (DAG levels / topological sort)
dsa.statement: n build components with prerequisite edges [u, v] (v cannot start until u finishes); each takes one time unit and all ready components build in parallel. Find the 'bottleneck' components — those that are the only component being built in their time step (i.e., singleton levels of the Kahn's-algorithm BFS). Variant: a parent→child DAG is given and you must invert it to find nodes executed alone at their level.
dsa.variant: Follow-ups: cycle detection, concurrent build tasks, complexity; Glassdoor 2023 'graphs and topological sort'.
dsa.evidence: India L5 onsite round 2 (2023-11), 1point3acres phone screen 'bottlenecks in dependency trees' (2025), OfferRetriever 'Bottleneck Dependencies', Glassdoor L4 Redmond (2023-08).

dsa.title: Web crawler with depth limit, then multithreaded
dsa.statement: Given a start URL and helpers fetch(url)/parse(html) → child URLs, crawl all reachable pages (LC 1236/1242 style). Follow-ups: restrict to depth K; explain why multithreading helps when fetch/parse are blocking; implement a thread-pool/queue version with a shared visited set and correct termination.
dsa.variant: Asked both as a 'design with code' round and as the System Programming round; interviewers probe thread-pool size, bottlenecks (network, disk), dataset size. Describing concurrency at a high level without code cost one India SDE-2 a 'strong hire'.
dsa.evidence: India SDE-2 onsite round 3 (2023-11), India L5 round 3 (2023-11), SDE3 LLD (2022), Blind 2023 'similar to LC 1242', Blind 2025 concurrency-round examples.

dsa.title: House Robber I → House Robber II (circular) → skip k houses
dsa.statement: Classic House Robber, then follow-ups as time allows: circular street (LC 213) and a generalisation where you must skip at least k houses between picks.
dsa.variant: interviewing.io notes difficulty increases as time allows; Bellevue new-grad screen got I then II.
dsa.evidence: New-grad phone screen Bellevue (2025-10), interviewing.io, Linkjob bank; LC 198/213 are the top DP items in Databricks' tag list.

dsa.title: Top-K frequent elements in a stream (variant)
dsa.statement: Maintain the K most frequent elements over a data stream with incremental updates (not a one-shot array). Discuss heap vs bucket/doubly-linked frequency list trade-offs and code one.
dsa.variant: Asked in the India SDE-2 phone screen; 'Kth largest in a metrics stream' (LC 703) is a related framing.
dsa.evidence: India SDE-2 phone round (2023-11); lastroundai lists LC 703 framing.

dsa.title: Longest mountain / peak in array with plateaus
dsa.statement: Part 1: find a peak element in a mountain array via binary search (LC 852). Part 2: in an array with multiple peaks and plateaus (equal neighbours), return the length of the longest peak, e.g. [1,2,3,3,4,5,4,3,6,4,2,1] → 5 for [3,6,4,2,1].
dsa.variant: Plateau handling is the twist versus LC 845.
dsa.evidence: India virtual rounds (2024-06); LC 845 is in Databricks' tagged list.

dsa.title: Minimum cost to visit all target nodes in a tree and return to root
dsa.statement: Given an undirected tree (not necessarily binary) with unit edge lengths and a set of target nodes, compute the minimum walk starting and ending at the root that visits every target: 2 × (number of edges in the minimal subtree spanning root and targets). Follow-up: you may start at any node (subtract the longest path within that subtree, i.e., its diameter-ish term).
dsa.evidence: Bengaluru campus SWE round 1 (Nov 2024, offer).

dsa.title: Minimum cost to cover all servers (choosing server i auto-covers the next i)
dsa.statement: N servers each have a cost; choosing server i (0-indexed) also covers the i servers after it, but you may still choose some of those. Find the minimum total cost to cover all servers. Start with O(n log n) and optimise to O(n).
dsa.evidence: Bengaluru campus SWE round 2 (Nov 2024, offer).

dsa.title: Iterate a binary tree with parent pointers in O(1) space
dsa.statement: TreeNode has left, right and parent pointers. Print/iterate all nodes in any order using constant extra space without modifying the tree (navigate via parent pointers, deciding direction based on where you came from).
dsa.variant: Older phone-screen classic; still a good warm-up for Databricks' iterator-heavy style.
dsa.evidence: Phone screen (2020-02), 13 comments.

dsa.title: Design String with sub-linear insert/delete/read
dsa.statement: Implement class NewString with read(index), insert(char, index), delete(index), all faster than O(n) — a rope / order-statistics balanced tree with subtree sizes.

dsa.title: Sparse matrix × vector multiplication
dsa.statement: Multiply a sparse matrix by a vector; re-represent the matrix (CSR / list of non-zeros) to make the operation time- and space-efficient.
dsa.evidence: Onsite coding round (2021-02).

dsa.title: In-place delta (incremental) encoding of an array, then distributed
dsa.statement: Encode an array in place so each element becomes the difference from its predecessor (keep the first element; process from the end backwards). Follow-up: do it when the array is sharded across a cluster (Spark-style) and does not fit in one machine's memory — each partition needs the last element of the previous partition.
dsa.evidence: New-grad onsite coding round (Linkjob, 2025–26).

dsa.title: OA: split array into K consecutive subarrays minimising sum of maxima
dsa.statement: Divide an array of N elements into K non-empty consecutive subarrays; cost of a subarray is its maximum; minimise total cost (N ≤ 300). Example [150,200,400,350,250], K=3 → 750. O(N²K) DP.
dsa.variant: OA problem (CodeSignal/HackerRank-style), new-grad pipeline.
dsa.evidence: Databricks OA 2024-02.

dsa.title: OA: cumulative bytes uploaded from overlapping segments
dsa.statement: Segments [start, end] (1-based, up to 1e18, may overlap/duplicate) arrive in order; after each, output the total number of distinct bytes received so far. Maintain a sorted set of disjoint intervals and merge on insert.
dsa.evidence: Databricks OA 2023-08.

dsa.title: OA: minimise (max − min) choosing one element per column/row
dsa.statement: Pick one element from each row (or each column of an N×M matrix) so that the difference between the maximum and minimum of the picked elements is minimised; return the min cost (or the sorted picked array). Sort all (value, row) pairs and slide a window that covers every row.
dsa.variant: Two reports: 2D array 'choose one per row, return sorted final array' (2023-02) and matrix 'start any row in col 1, jump to any row in next column' (OA 2023-10).
dsa.evidence: Databricks interview question (2023-02) and OA (2023-10).

dsa.title: OA: maximum prefix-removal operations with at most K unique chars after one edit
dsa.statement: Repeatedly remove the longest prefix containing at most K distinct characters; return the maximum number of operations if you may change at most one character of S (|S| ≤ 1e4). Brute force over 26·|S| edits TLEs — reason about where a change can split a run.
dsa.evidence: Databricks OA 2023-10.

dsa.title: Division in an unfamiliar assembly-like language (LLVM IR)
dsa.statement: Given a short reference for an assembly-like language (LLVM IR: alloca/store/load, add/sub, icmp/br) and a skeleton program, implement integer division returning quotient and remainder by repeated subtraction, then debug/test it. Tests ability to learn an unfamiliar language from docs under time pressure.
dsa.variant: Historic 'Coding, Debugging, Testing' round (2020–2021); not reported since 2022 but illustrates Databricks' practical style.
dsa.evidence: Onsite reports 2021-05 and 2021-02.

dsa.title: Decode Ways with a variation
dsa.statement: Classic Decode Ways, then the interviewer changes the constraints mid-problem (variation on the mapping).
dsa.evidence: SWE II phone screen (2020-07, Glassdoor).

dsa.title: Design a data structure with 3 methods meeting runtime requirements (phone screen class design)
dsa.statement: Phone-screen style: implement a class with several methods whose time bounds are specified up front (e.g., O(1) insert/delete/getRandom or an ordered-access structure); the candidate used Python datetime, suggesting a time-windowed variant.
dsa.variant: Reported generically (SWE II screen, 2026-07); treat as the family of 'design a class with runtime constraints' questions Databricks favours.
dsa.evidence: Glassdoor SWE II phone screen (2026-07).

dsa.title: Merge K sorted logs into one time-ordered stream
dsa.statement: Merge k time-sorted execution-log streams into one ordered stream with a min-heap (O(N log k)); framed in Databricks' logs/data-pipeline language.
dsa.evidence: Listed in lastroundai's Databricks question set; LC 23 is a standard warm-up for Databricks' iterator/stream problems.

dsa.title: Longest palindrome by concatenating two-letter words (OA)
dsa.statement: Given two-letter words, build the longest palindrome by concatenating a subset (LC 2131).
dsa.variant: Appeared in the 2021 OA; LC 2131 is still in Databricks' tagged list.
dsa.evidence: Databricks OA 'Longest Palindrome with Pairs' (2021-10).

design.title: Online bookstore / lowest-price book aggregator
design.prompt: Design a middleman service: a user searches a book (ISBN) with a max price and payment method; the service fans out to 50–200 (or hundreds of) seller APIs with 10–20 s latency, returns the lowest price, and purchases if under the user's max. Variant: a full online bookseller with browsing/search, inventory, orders, payment and order-state tracking.
probes: fan-out with timeouts and partial results
dedupe by ISBN, caching and price freshness
why POST not GET for the pricing endpoint
DB insert succeeds but SQS publish fails → transactional outbox
duplicate messages under at-least-once → idempotent consumers
search and purchase flows end to end
design.round: Architecture (60 min) and increasingly the Architecture-style phone screen
design.evidence: Reported in at least 7 loops 2025–2026: Staff AI-platform loop (asked twice), L6→L5 loop (phone screen AND onsite), 2026-08 design screen (passed), 2026-05 screen, 2026-07 offer loop onsite 5, interviewing.io, Linkjob.

design.title: Chat / Slack-like messaging system (with message deletion)
design.prompt: Design a real-time messaging app (direct + group/channel messages, history, offline catch-up). Variant asked at senior full-stack: Slack-style app that supports deleting messages/threads while sends are racing.
probes: API design and DB schema for conversations/messages
message flow send → store → deliver (fan-out, WebSockets)
ordering and consistency contract when deletion races a send across servers
surprisingly little scaling discussion in some rounds — focus on correctness
design.evidence: Onsite 2026-09 (chat APIs/storage), 2026-07 cleared-onsite loop, 2026 senior full-stack (Slack with deletion), India virtual rounds 2024-06 (WhatsApp/Slack), PracHub bank entries 2025-10 and 2026-05.

design.title: Payment processing system (Visa-like / game-platform credit card)
design.prompt: Design a card payment system: validate cards, route by card number to issuers, handle authorisation/capture, refunds, credits and in-game items for an online game platform. Scope choice (network vs merchant gateway) is part of the question.
probes: concurrent transactions on one account and failure recovery (interviewer dug very deep)
design.evidence: Senior onsite 2026-04 (credit-card processing for a game platform; 'spent half the interview on concurrent transactions'), Linkjob 'Payment Gateway', PracHub Visa-style entries (2026-02, 2026-09).

design.title: Distributed / dependency-aware job scheduler
design.prompt: Design a job scheduler (think Spark job scheduling or Google Borg): submit jobs with dependencies and resource needs, schedule across a cluster, handle failures and retries.
probes: fault tolerance of the scheduler itself (leader election, state store)
design.evidence: Blind 2025-11 ('Design job scheduler, think Borg'), PracHub 'dependency-aware job scheduler' (2026-01), lastroundai 'distributed Spark job scheduler'.

design.title: Music playlist service
design.prompt: Design a playlist service: create playlists, add/remove/reorder tracks, deterministic playback order, retry-safe operations. Asked as the (misdescribed) 'full-stack system design' phone screen.
probes: ordering model for reorders (fractional indexes / linked list)
design.evidence: Phone screen in 2026-07 loop (passed); PracHub bank entry (2026-07).

design.title: Distributed / hierarchical file system (scope it yourself)
design.prompt: Design a distributed file system with a hierarchical namespace; requirements deliberately vague — scope them (metadata vs data separation, inode-like structures, replication, consensus).
design.round: Architecture / Storage (phone screen for staff backend; onsite otherwise)
design.evidence: PracHub entries 2026-03 and 2026-09 (staff backend phone screen); a Bangalore design interviewer described building a new file system at Databricks.

design.title: Distributed rate limiter / throttling across client → gateway → API → DB
design.prompt: Design throttling for millions of requests per second across a chain client → gateway → API server → DB/third-party: rate limiting, backpressure, circuit breakers, request prioritisation.
design.round: Architecture (60 min); single-machine multi-threaded version appears in System Programming
design.evidence: Linkjob 'Throttle System Safety', lastroundai 'distributed rate limiter', Blind 2024-12 concurrency-round example 'rate limiter', Blind 2023 'rate limiter with single machine and multiple threads'.

design.title: Add delete + trash to a database server API, then optimise for production
design.prompt: Given a simple database/API server, extend it with delete and trash (soft delete, restore, purge) functionality and discuss production optimisation. New-grad architecture round framed as 'modify a simple API to support new features'.
design.evidence: Linkjob new-grad onsite (2025–26); Glassdoor new-grad Mountain View (2025-12) 'modify a simple API to support new features'.

design.title: Stock order manager reconciling with an external broker API
design.prompt: Design a service that manages stock order lifecycle (placed → filled/cancelled) and reconciles state with an external exchange API that can time out or respond late.

design.title: CRUD APIs with asynchronous background jobs
design.prompt: Design CRUD operations whose expensive side-effects run as asynchronous background jobs; expose job status.
probes: consistency between resource state and job state

design.title: Digital game shop backend
design.prompt: Design the backend for a digital game store: catalogue, purchases, entitlements, payments.

design.title: Version-controlled diary / Google-Docs-like document
design.prompt: Design a personal diary with one entry per day containing ordered mixed content (text, images, URLs, tables, video); users can edit past entries, every change autosaves every 10 s, and version history must be browsable like Google Docs.

design.title: Ingestion pipeline with queryable real-time events / feature store
design.prompt: Design a pipeline that ingests high-throughput events and makes them queryable in near real time (partitioned log, small-batch atomic commits, compaction); or a feature store serving batch training and online inference.
design.evidence: lastroundai Databricks design set; aligns with Databricks' Stream Processing module in the official prep PDF.

design.title: Type-ahead / autocomplete with retries, debouncing and caching (full-stack systems round)
design.prompt: Build/design an autocomplete component: retry logic, debouncing, latest-request-wins cancellation, client-side caching; implementation expected (full-stack 'Front-End Systems' round).

design.title: RAG retrieval for data assets / coding agent (ML system design)
design.prompt: Design retrieval for an assistant over enterprise data assets or a codebase: what to index, hybrid exact + semantic search, handling noisy content, evaluation metrics.
probes: chunking and embeddings vs metadata filters
design.evidence: PracHub entries (2026-05, 2026-09) tied to AI-platform roles; FDE loops ask transformer architecture in depth.

lld.title: Durable single-node key-value store (WAL, recovery, batching)
lld.prompt: Design a single-machine (explicitly NOT distributed) durable KV store: put/get/delete where a successful put guarantees the data survives process crash or power loss. Write pseudocode for the write path, log format, recovery and compaction; discuss fsync policy and batching.
lld.deliverable: Pseudocode + data structures in CoderPad; trade-off discussion
probes: WAL record/segment format and fsync-before-ack vs bounded loss window
group commit / batching to amortise fsync (asked three times in one loop)
crash recovery and torn writes, checksums, atomic file install
compaction/GC of stale versions and tombstones
how recovered state differs if evictions are logged
scale to 100× load: what saturates first
lld.evidence: Bangalore L4 design round (2024-05), Bengaluru L4 (2024-10, 'async write every 100th put'), onsite 2021-02, Staff loop 2026-05 (concurrent KV with batch writes), PracHub 'durable KV store' (2025-08) and 'KV store I'd never seen' screen (2025-11), Blind 2022–2023 posts.

lld.title: Thread-safe durable event/log writer with batching
lld.prompt: Implement an EventWriter/Logger where thousands of threads call appendEvent(bytes) to write to ONE file with high throughput, low latency and durability (return only after data is on disk). Start synchronous, then make it multi-threaded while preserving order.
probes: naive mutex + write + fsync per event and why it is slow
producer–consumer: locked queue + single writer thread
batch drain + one write() + one fsync() per batch
promise/future (or condition variable) so each appendEvent blocks until its batch is durable
OS page cache and fsync semantics
lld.evidence: L4 offer loop round 4 (2025-06), senior onsite LLD (2026-04), offer loop onsite 2 (2026-07), L6→L5 'log writer' (2026-09), Staff loop 'log writer + WAL batching' (2026-05), interviewing.io 'efficient logger', PracHub entries 2025-12/2026-02/2026-07/2026-09.

lld.title: Single-node persistent in-memory cache (LRU, byte capacity, sharded locks, TTL)
lld.prompt: Design a single-machine cache for a web service with many worker threads: Get/Put/Delete in ~O(1), eviction (LRU) by byte capacity, optional durability via WAL/snapshots, no disk I/O inside critical sections. Variant: thread-safe LRU with TTL expiry.
lld.deliverable: Data structures + pseudocode APIs + lock design
probes: hash map + intrusive doubly linked list, why nodes store their key
global lock → striped/sharded locks (per-shard LRU trade-off)
Get mutates recency so it writes under lock; shrink critical sections
deadlock-freedom invariant for multi-key ops (lock ordering)
expiration-aware eviction, lock contention at high QPS
value larger than a shard, reader racing eviction, hot keys
lld.round: System Programming (60 min) or Architecture-style phone screen (new grad)
lld.evidence: PracHub technical screen (2026-01, new grad) and bank entries (2026-05 'WAL persistence, sharded locks and LRU'), Linkjob onsite concurrency round (thread-safe LRU with TTL), lastroundai, Blind concurrency-round examples ('cache lib').

lld.title: CachedFile: range-aware caching client over a remote StorageClient
lld.prompt: Given StorageClient.getFileSize(uri) and fetch(uri, offset, length, buffer), design CachedFile so many clients can read arbitrary [start,end) byte ranges of a remote file with minimal repeated network calls and efficient repeated reads.
probes: chunk/bucket the file into fixed-size blocks and cache per block (memory/disk)
fetch each block at most once; coalesce overlapping requests
thread pool to fetch blocks in parallel
duplicate fetches across threads (in-flight map), failures/retries
lld.evidence: SDE-II onsite round 4 (2026-02); PracHub 'concurrent range-aware file caching client' (2025-08).

lld.title: Circuit breaker for a leader/follower (primary + replicas) database gateway
lld.prompt: A gateway routes reads/writes to a primary and replica databases, each guarded by its own circuit breaker: after N consecutive errors (e.g. 2) the breaker opens and blocks traffic; after a cooldown of consecutive blocked requests it closes again. Implement routing with fallback from primary to secondary and recovery, following a long list of given rules.
probes: fallback order and what happens when all are open
code quality under a long spec
lld.evidence: India SDE-2 onsite round 2 (2023-11); OfferRetriever 'Circuit Breaker'; PracHub 'circuit-breaker-aware database routing' (2026-08).

lld.title: Bounded producer–consumer queue / thread pool
lld.prompt: Implement a thread pool where producer threads enqueue work and worker threads block waiting for items; or a bounded multi-producer multi-consumer queue with timeouts and fairness. Then discuss deadlocks and how to avoid/debug them.
lld.deliverable: Pseudocode or runnable code with locks and condition variables
probes: lock ordering to avoid deadlock, debugging a deadlock
lld.evidence: Blind 2021 example questions (thread pool, deadlock), Blind 2022 'producer consumer problems', PracHub 'thread-safe bounded queue' (2025-09), L4 Blind 2025-09 concurrency round ('threadpools, multithreading and events').

lld.title: Multithreaded web crawler with depth limit
lld.prompt: Crawl from a seed URL using provided fetch/parse helpers up to depth K, then parallelise with a thread pool and shared visited set; explain where threads help and how to size the pool.
lld.deliverable: Code for BFS, then multithreaded version (expected for strong hire)
probes: thread pool size vs dataset size
lld.evidence: India SDE-2 (2023-11), India L5 (2023-11), SDE3 LLD (2022), Blind 2023 and 2025 concurrency-round examples.

lld.title: Thread-safe KV store + hit counter: identify and fix race conditions
lld.prompt: Take the in-memory KV store with QPS/hit counting and make it correct under many concurrent threads; identify races in the given implementation and fix them. Includes the conceptual probe: why is HashMap not thread-safe, how does ConcurrentHashMap lock, what is CAS.
probes: read-write lock vs striped locks vs ConcurrentHashMap
lld.evidence: Blind 'Confusing experience' thread (interviewer spent 50 min on ConcurrentHashMap internals), PracHub 'identify and handle race conditions' (2025-09), lastroundai conceptual list, 2026-07 loop 'KV store with hit counter, many follow-ups'.

lld.title: Per-key rate-limited KV store (5-minute query threshold) / single-machine multi-threaded rate limiter
lld.prompt: Build an in-memory KV store that limits how often each key may be queried in a 5-minute window to protect hot keys; or implement a rate limiter on a single machine accessed by multiple threads.
probes: sliding window vs token bucket per key
memory for many keys (eviction of idle limiters)
thread safety per key without a global lock
lld.evidence: PracHub bank (2026-09), Blind concurrency-round example 'rate limiter' (2024-12), Blind 2023 'rate limiter single machine multiple threads'.

lld.title: Query-plan tree optimiser: column pruning and filter pushdown
lld.prompt: Given a SQL query plan represented as a tree of operators (scan, filter, project, join), implement rewrite rules such as predicate/filter pushdown and column pruning; the interviewer does not say which optimisations to apply.
probes: which pushdowns are safe across joins
lld.round: Coding / Software Engineering Fundamentals (new grad onsite, 60 min)
lld.evidence: PracHub new-grad entries (2026-01 'brutal SQL query optimization round', 2026-09).

lld.title: Parking lot class design (HM screen, India)
lld.prompt: Classic parking lot LLD with a short set of clear requirements; produce a class diagram during the hiring-manager conversation.
lld.evidence: India virtual rounds (2024-06); Blind 2022 commenter referenced 'design a parking lot' style for the CoderPad design round.

lld.title: Small CRUD app / take-home API integration (full-stack & some India teams)
lld.prompt: Build a small CRUD app in 45 min (Node/React) or a take-home integrating an external weather-forecast API into a service with tests (3–5 h, any language).
lld.round: Take-home or practical coding (not in standard backend loops)
lld.evidence: Bengaluru senior SWE (2024-04, Taro), India virtual rounds (2024-06), interviewing.io notes rare ~5 h take-homes.
